li.a: The Age: Melbourne remembers Queen St massacre (6 December 2007)
The Age: Survivors, families relive the agony of Queen Street (9 December 2007)
Monument Australia: Australian Post and Telecom Credit Union Victims Memorial
Public Record Office Victoria: Gun laws in 1980s Victoria
Crime+Investigation: Could the Queen Street Massacre Happen Today?

content.p: Shortly after four in the afternoon on 8 December 1987, a 22-year-old man walked into the Australia Post offices at 191 Queen Street, in Melbourne's central business district, carrying a sawn-off rifle in a paper bag. He had come to kill a former schoolmate. When that man got away, the gunman began shooting office workers at random. Within a short time eight people were dead, and five more had been wounded. The gunman was stopped by two employees, and when he tried to escape along a ledge he fell from the 11th floor and died.

The Age, writing on the twentieth anniversary, called it Australia's biggest mass killing at the time. It came four months after another Melbourne gunman, Julian Knight, shot seven people in Hoddle Street, Clifton Hill. Together the two cases strengthened the Victorian government's plan to license and register firearms, and that plan drew organised opposition.
content.h2: A visit meant for one man
content.p: The Age described Frank Vitkovic as a failed law student. On the afternoon of 8 December he entered the Australia Post building with a sawn-off rifle, meaning to find Con Margelis, a former schoolmate. Margelis got out of the way. The shooting that followed was not aimed at anyone in particular, and the first person killed was Judith Morris, who was on the fifth floor.

The Age reported that the 22-year-old then went on firing on the 12th floor and then on the 11th. The dead included Nancy Vignone and Rodney Brown. Catherine Dowling and Julie McBean died too, and so did Michael McGuire, Marianne Van Ewyk and David Spencer. Julie McBean was 20. She had worked at Australia Post for only nine months and was in line for a promotion. David Spencer was the partner and co-worker of postal worker Sue Welfare, who survived the shooting. He was killed, leaving her to raise their two small children. The name spelled Vignone in the 6 December article is spelled Avignone in the 9 December article, and the two pieces do not agree on the spelling.
content.h2: The two men who stopped him
content.p: The Age described how Tony Gioia, who was 165 centimetres tall, tackled the tall, burly Vitkovic so that Frank Carmody could take the gun. Carmody, a clerk in the finance department, had already been shot four times, once in the back. He took the gun and ended the shooting. Both men were later awarded the Star of Courage, Australia's second-highest bravery decoration. Monument Australia, which describes the memorial window, says the gunman was overpowered by workers, one of whom was wounded, and that two of them later received the Star of Courage while two more received commendations for bravery.

Speaking on the twentieth anniversary, Carmody told The Age that he rarely relived the day. He said that the events of other mass shootings, including one in Omaha, Nebraska, brought the memories back. "I imagine how the people are feeling, locked in and enclosed with a gunman coming at them," he said. He had lost touch with Gioia and other former workmates in recent years.

How Vitkovic came to fall from the building is one of the points on which the accounts differ. The Age's first article said he plunged 11 floors to his death. Its second article, published three days later, said he leapt from the 11th floor. Monument Australia gives a different sequence. In its account, he climbed onto a window ledge while trying to escape, kicked free of a worker who was trying to stop him, and fell. The detective Colin McLaren, who was the first police officer at the scene, watched the body strike the footpath. The Age reported that the body struck the footpath with such force that it bounced about a metre from the ground.

McLaren also said that the people inside the building were badly shaken. "Many people were dead and the rest injured, some were hysterical, screaming or cowering under their desks, or clutching at each other in the corners of the office," he said. He told The Age that he heard as many as 100 rounds fired in about 10 minutes. That is his own estimate of the firing.

Monument Australia reports that a forensic psychologist, given as Dr Allen Batholomew, gave evidence at the coronial hearing that the gunman had been criminally insane at the time of the shooting. Among the pages cited here, only Monument Australia reports this, so it should be read as one account rather than as settled.
The Age's 2007 pieces do not mention an insanity finding, and neither does the Public Record Office Victoria page.
content.h2: A year of shootings in Melbourne
content.p: The Public Record Office Victoria describes 1987 as a year of six mass shootings across Australia, two of them in Melbourne. In August Julian Knight used a Ruger rifle, an M14 and a Mossberg shotgun to fire on drivers and police in Hoddle Street. He killed seven people and injured 19. Four months later Vitkovic used a modified M1 to shoot office workers on Queen Street. The archive's account says he shot 13 people and killed eight of them.

The Victorian government of John Cain had announced firearms reform in 1981, as part of Labor's priorities for the 1982 election. Its policy was a licensing and registration system, so that gun owners would have to do more than pay a fee to obtain a firearm. The Public Record Office Victoria says the 1987 and 1988 shootings strengthened that commitment. The Firearms (Prohibited Weapons) Regulations banned semi-automatic weapons, and the Firearms (Amendment) Bill brought in licensing and registration, with heavier penalties for non-compliance.

The reform was not uncontested. A departmental brief records the opposition's argument that the government was "grandstanding" on the Hoddle Street killings. It reports that in 1988 about 30,000 gun enthusiasts took to the streets against the proposed rules, and that the opposition leader, Jeff Kennett, warned that most semi-automatic owners would not give up their guns, which would create a black market. A government statement on the bill put the number of such rifles in Victoria at about 210,000 and said owners would be required to surrender them for compensation.

The archive also quotes the historian Nick Brodie, author of a study of Australia's gun control history, who said that the public had generally been supportive of sensible gun laws, but that by the 1980s organised lobby groups were driving the debate in the press.
content.h2: Later reform and the wider question
content.p: Crime+Investigation, writing about whether a Queen Street-style attack could happen again, describes the Queen Street shootings as part of a run of random killings in Australia that began with the Top End shootings in June 1987. It argues that the decisive change came after the Port Arthur massacre at the Tasmanian resort in April 1996, when a new national firearms agreement banned rapid-fire long guns, introduced a compulsory buyback, and required a genuine reason to own a weapon. The article also notes that the question of whether the reforms have worked is debated.

For the twentieth anniversary in 2007, the survivors and families asked Australia Post not to hold a public memorial. Instead a low-key private wreath-laying was to be held at the window in the old GPO building, where Elizabeth and Bourke streets meet. The window honours eight Australia Post and Telecom Credit Union colleagues, all killed at work on 8 December 1987.

On the anniversary day, about 50 people attended a memorial service at 191 Queen Street, where the names of the dead were read aloud. The Age reported that parents and children, brothers and sisters, co-workers and friends gathered there. Irene McBean went to her eldest daughter's grave in the morning and then to the spot where Julie was shot, which by then was a block of apartments. Australia Post spokesperson Nadine Lyford said, "This was a tragic day that touched many of Australia Post's employees and their families and friends."

The death toll is the simplest point of agreement. Eight people were killed by the gunman. Monument Australia counts nine dead including the gunman, and gives five injured. The archive's figures of 13 people shot and eight killed leave five wounded, which matches that count.

The circumstances of the fall are not agreed. The Age gives two accounts within three days of each other, one of a plunge and one of a leap. Monument Australia gives a third, of climbing onto a ledge and kicking free of a worker. The sources also differ on one victim's name, given as Nancy Vignone in the 6 December article and Annunziata Avignone in the 9 December article. The psychologist's name appears only on the Monument Australia page, and the coronial finding is reported by that source alone.
